deep.reconstruction:
Context. This page belongs to Riemann's fragment on the boundary behaviour of the elliptic modular functions. The fragment was published posthumously as 'Fragmente über die Grenzfälle der elliptischen Modulfunctionen' (Werke 1876, XXVIII), with Dedekind's 1892 Erläuterungen. Formulas 48-59 are q-series for log k, log k', log(2K/pi), and so on. Formulas 62 ff. give the values of the integrals of these series, taken along a radius, at the boundary point q0 = e^{ix}. Each value is written as a real part (a log-cos or log-tan series) plus an imaginary part (a series with the sawtooth function ((y)), which is 0 at half-integers).

Setting from the previous page (formula 62). The real part is
R(x) = sum_{nu != 0} (-1)^nu log(4 cos^2(nu x/2)) / nu^2 - 2 log4 * (1 - 1/4 + 1/9 - ...).
Here the sum runs over all nonzero integers, so it equals 2 * sum_{nu >= 1}.

First sentence of this page. The imaginary part converges for every x, since its terms are bounded sawtooth values divided by nu^2. The real part is treated only at rational points x/(2pi) = m/n with gcd(m,n) = 1. The footnote says that for irrational ('surd') x it does not converge.

Method (implicit; my reconstruction). Put nu = s + n t. Then log(4cos^2(nu m pi/n)) depends only on s mod n. Use the partial fractions (Euler):
- sum_t (-1)^t/(z+t)^2 = pi^2 cos(pi z)/sin^2(pi z);
- sum_t 1/(z+t)^2 = pi^2/sin^2(pi z).

1° n odd. Here (-1)^{s+nt} = (-1)^s (-1)^t. This gives
sum_{nu != 0} (-1)^nu log(4cos^2(nu m pi/n))/nu^2 = (pi^2/n^2) * sum_{s=1}^{n-1} (-1)^s [cos(pi s/n)/sin^2(pi s/n)] log(4cos^2(s m pi/n)) - (pi^2/(6 n^2)) log 4.
The last term comes from s = n, i.e. nu = n t: sum_{t != 0} (-1)^t/(n^2 t^2) = -pi^2/(6 n^2).

2° n even (so m is odd). Here (-1)^{s+nt} = (-1)^s, and the s and n-s terms coincide. This gives
(pi^2/n^2) * sum_{s=1}^{n/2-1} 2(-1)^s log(4cos^2(s m pi/n))/sin^2(pi s/n) + (pi^2/(3 n^2)) log 4 + (singular class s = n/2).
The singular class is nu = (n/2) p with p odd. There cos(nu m pi/n) = 0, so the term is log 0. Riemann regularises it by keeping q = r q0 inside the radius:
- the terms become (16/n^2)(-1)^{n/2} * sum_{p odd > 0} log(1 - r^{np/2})/p^2;
- with eps = 1 - r, this is ~ (16/n^2)(-1)^{n/2} [(pi^2/8)(log eps + log n - log 2) + sum log p/p^2];
- this equals (2pi^2/n^2)(-1)^{n/2} [log((q0-q)/(q0+q)) + log n + (8/pi^2) sum_{p odd} log p/p^2], since log((q0-q)/(q0+q)) ~ log(eps/2).

This is exactly Riemann's formula. His conclusion: after subtracting (2pi^2/n^2)(-1)^{n/2} log((q0-q)/(q0+q)), the function tends to a finite limit as q -> q0 (q approaching in a fixed manner), and the formula gives that limit.

Formula 63. -log k' = 8 sum_{j odd} sum_{n>=1} q^{(2n-1)j}/j. Integrating against dq/q gives
4 sum_{j odd} j^{-2} log((1+q^j)/(1-q^j)).
At q = e^{ix} we have (1+q^j)/(1-q^j) = i cot(jx/2), so the real part is
-2 sum_{j odd > 0} log(tan^2(jx/2))/j^2 = -2 log tg^2(x/2) - (2/9) log tg^2(3x/2) - (2/25) log tg^2(5x/2) - ...
The imaginary part, with sawtooth terms, is continued on the next page.
errors: Formula 63 is written with -log k on this page. The tan-series is correct only for -log k', which is how the next page writes it, so this is a slip.
The constant in case 1° appears as pi^2/(6^2 n^2) log 4. The correct value is pi^2/(6 n^2) log 4: sum_{t != 0} (-1)^t/(n t)^2 = -pi^2/(6n^2). This is likely a misreading or stray mark.

Footnote: the claim that the real-part series does not converge for every irrational x is false as stated. For badly approximable x (e.g. quadratic irrationals divided by 2pi), |cos(nu x/2)| >> 1/nu, so the terms are O(log nu/nu^2) and the series converges. It fails only for x with very good rational approximations (a measure-zero set), unless Riemann means non-existence of a regular limit in some other sense.

In case 2°, interchanging the limit r -> 1 with the infinite sum over p is not justified on the page. The step is nevertheless correct, by dominated convergence, since log(1-e^{-a}) - log a -> 0 as a -> 0 and is controlled for large a.

results.what: Closed form of sum_{nu != 0} (-1)^nu log(4cos^2(nu pi m/n))/nu^2 at rational points, via residue classes mod n and Euler's partial fractions, n odd
results.modern_name: Evaluation of a Lambert/Eisenstein-type series at a cusp (radial limit at a root of unity)

results.what: Singular asymptotics as q -> q0 for n even: logarithmic singularity log((q0-q)/(q0+q)) with explicit finite part involving log n and sum log p/p^2 over odd p
results.modern_name: Asymptotic expansion of a modular integral near a cusp
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann, Fragment XXVIII; analysed by Dedekind 1892

results.what: Formula 63: integral from 0 to e^{ix} of -log k' dq/q = -2 sum_{j odd} log tan^2(jx/2)/j^2 (+ imaginary sawtooth part)
results.modern_name: Boundary values of integrated theta-quotient q-series

results.what: Partial fractions sum (-1)^t/(z+t)^2 = pi^2 cos(pi z)/sin^2(pi z) and sum 1/(z+t)^2 = pi^2/sin^2(pi z)

deep.surprise_reason: This page is part of Riemann's fragment on the limiting cases of the modular functions, published in his Werke (1876) and famously commented on by Dedekind, where Dedekind sums originated. The content is known as Riemann's. The page shows draft details and a constant slip, but no new result.

transcription_corrections: 'pi^2/(6^2 n^2) log 4' in 1° should read pi^2/(6 n^2) log 4 (mathematically required).
The summation limits in 1° are s = 1 to n-1; in 2° they are s = 1 to n/2 - 1.
In 2°, p denotes an odd number and the sum sum log p/p^2 runs over odd p (positive).
Formula 63's integrand should be -log k' (as on the next page), not -log k.
The opening words are possibly 'Pars imaginaria hujus seriei convergit ...'; read as 'the imaginary part of the series converges for every x; the real part*, ... can be expressed thus'.
